reference.source: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders / IUIS classification of inborn errors of immunity
clinicalPearls: Presents as a combined immunodeficiency with severe eczema, markedly raised serum IgE and profound eosinophilia, distinguishing it from the autosomal dominant STAT3 (Job) syndrome

Hallmark is susceptibility to widespread and treatment-resistant cutaneous viral infection, particularly recurrent herpes simplex, molluscum contagiosum, human papillomavirus warts and varicella zoster
Recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infection occurs but, unlike STAT3-HIES, pneumatoceles and connective-tissue or skeletal features are typically absent
There is a high lifetime risk of malignancy, especially virally driven squamous cell carcinoma and lymphoma, which is a leading cause of death
Severe food and environmental allergy, asthma and anaphylaxis are common because of the profound T-helper-2 skewing
Neurological complications including CNS vasculitis and infective encephalitis may occur and carry a poor outcome
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive treatment and can reverse the immunodeficiency and atopic phenotype
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating absent DOCK8 protein by flow cytometry or biallelic loss-of-function variants on genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: DOCK8 encodes a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor that regulates the actin cytoskeleton, and its loss impairs the shape integrity and migration of lymphocytes through dense tissue such as skin. Affected T and NK cells undergo cytoskeleton-dependent cell death (cytothripsis) as they move, causing progressive loss of memory T cells and defective cytotoxicity against virally infected keratinocytes. Impaired dendritic-cell and lymphocyte function produces a combined immunodeficiency with poor antibody memory, while unopposed T-helper-2 responses drive the very high IgE, eosinophilia and severe atopic disease. The result is the characteristic triad of recalcitrant cutaneous viral infection, allergic disease and heightened cancer risk.
additionalDifferentials: Severe atopic dermatitis with recurrent infection
Omenn syndrome and other combined immunodeficiencies
IPEX and other severe immune dysregulation syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Flow cytometry for DOCK8 protein expression in lymphocytes
Serum immunoglobulins showing very high IgE with variable IgM and specific antibody deficiency
Full blood count and differential documenting marked eosinophilia and lymphopenia
Lymphocyte subset enumeration with reduced memory T and B cells and impaired NK function
Lymphocyte proliferation and vaccine antibody response assays
Next-generation sequencing or targeted DOCK8 gene analysis including copy-number assessment for large deletions
redFlags: New or enlarging cutaneous lesion suggesting virally driven squamous cell carcinoma
Lymphadenopathy, weight loss or cytopenias raising concern for lymphoma
Neurological deficit indicating CNS vasculitis or infective encephalitis
reference.prognosis: Untreated DOCK8 deficiency carries a poor prognosis with early mortality from infection, malignancy or vascular complications. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, particularly when performed before serious complications develop, can be curative and markedly improves survival.
pitfalls: Misclassifying it as ordinary severe atopic dermatitis and delaying immunological evaluation
Confusing it with autosomal dominant STAT3 hyper-IgE, which has a very different management and prognosis
Underestimating the malignancy risk and failing to survey the skin and lymphoid tissue
Attributing recurrent skin viral infection to poor hygiene rather than an underlying immunodeficiency
Delaying referral for transplantation until irreversible organ or CNS damage has occurred
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
